note: Mock content for the prototype. The ship and its history are invented.

core.text: This is a model of the Marigold, the ship the figurehead came from. It was built at one forty-eighth of the real size by a shipwright who had worked on the ship itself.
The Marigold was a three-masted barque. She carried timber and grain across the Atlantic with a crew of about fourteen, and a crossing took around five weeks.
Every rope on the model is a real, working line, tied the way it would have been on the ship. The sailors had to know each of these by touch, often in the dark.

open_question.text: Where on the ship do you think the crew slept?

additions.text: Here's a detail in the rigging: there are over two hundred separate lines on this model, and each sail needed four or five of them just to raise it.
Look along the bottom of the hull. The copper colour is copper sheeting, which stopped worms from boring into the wood.
A little more on how the real ship was built: the frame went up first, like a skeleton, and then planks were steamed so they would bend around it. Building her took about a year.
Right at the front, under the bowsprit, you can see a tiny version of the figurehead we just saw, in her original position.
The ship's compass sat just in front of the wheel, here at the back. The real one is on display across the room.

qa.text: The real ship was about 40 metres long, so this model is roughly 48 times smaller.
About fourteen. Most of them slept in hammocks in the front of the ship, below deck.
She was broken up for timber around 1880, after nearly thirty years of sailing. The figurehead was saved.

qa_fallback.text: That's a good question, and I don't know the answer. What we do know is that she sailed for nearly thirty years.
